title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can support second-language (L2) learners’ critical thinking and argumentative essay writing. The authors frame the problem around the difficulty L2 learners face in producing strong argumentative writing, especially in connecting critical thinking processes with essay structure. To address this, they develop a proposed instructional model, the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW), based on the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model, Tan’s argumentative writing framework, and Hattie and Timperley’s feedback model.

The empirical component is a small quantitative experiment comparing two groups using ChatGPT under different conditions. The experimental group used ChatGPT with the CGCAW prompt guidelines, while the control group used ChatGPT freely without those guidelines. Participants were asked to write a 150-300 word argumentative essay in 40 minutes on whether social media is beneficial or harmful to society. Essays were scored by three evaluators: Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a university course instructor, using partly different criteria.

The study involved 10 second-language learners from a single state university, randomly assigned into two groups of five. The writing session was conducted under monitored conditions via video conferencing, and the completed essays were submitted by email. Although the paper states random assignment, the sample is extremely small, and two participants in the experimental group were excluded from the authors’ final calculations because they could not complete the task within the allotted time, indicating instability in implementation and analysis.

Findings were mixed rather than uniformly positive. ChatGPT-based scoring slightly favored the experimental group on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, but Grammarly and especially the course instructor favored the control group. The instructor’s mean scores were much higher for the control group than the experimental group, suggesting the CGCAW framework may have hindered performance on core argumentative features such as thesis and summary under the time-constrained conditions. The paper does not report motivation outcomes, no writing pretest-posttest design is used, and no credible large effect size is presented. This is not the alleged 2026 high-school 25+25 student 12-week motivation RCT; it is a very small undergraduate one-session writing experiment and should not be treated as evidence for large quantitative effects in high-school ChatGPT writing feedback synthesis.
quality_tier_rationale: Although the paper claims random assignment, it is a tiny university pilot (n=10) with post-randomization exclusion of 2 experimental participants, inconsistent outcome calculation, no inferential statistics, no preregistration, and non-independent/partly AI-based grading. It is not the alleged high-school 25+25 RCT and does not provide credible effect estimates for synthesis.
impact_tier_rationale: Observed impacts are unclear and inconsistent across raters: small descriptive advantages for the experimental group on some ChatGPT-scored dimensions but worse performance under instructor and Grammarly assessments. No credible standardized effect size can be supported, and there is no motivation result at all.

interventions.use_case: Students used ChatGPT during a one-session argumentative essay task; the experimental group used a structured ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW) and the control group used ChatGPT freely without guidelines.
Grammarly was used as an automated writing assessment/scoring tool to evaluate essay correctness, clarity, engagement, and delivery.
ChatGPT itself was also used as an essay evaluator, scoring clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, and persuasiveness for all student essays.

finding.finding_summary: This was a very small university L2 writing experiment (10 participants randomized to 5 experimental and 5 control, though the authors then excluded 2 experimental students from final calculations). For writing quality, ChatGPT scoring slightly favored the experimental CGCAW group (mean total 74.0 vs 72.2; reported SDs 7.6 vs 5.5), but the course instructor strongly favored the control group (mean 35 vs 56), and Grammarly also slightly favored the control group (90.6 vs 92.2). No inferential statistics, no valid pooled effect size, and no motivation outcome were reported.
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality scored by ChatGPT rubric, course instructor rubric, and Grammarly
finding.study_size: n=10 total (5+5 assigned); authors state Participant 3 and 5 in experimental group were excluded from final calculations, creating inconsistent analytic sample
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT total scores: experimental SD=7.6, control SD=5.5

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames the intervention as improving critical thinking through argumentative writing, but critical thinking was not directly measured with a validated instrument. Instead, the authors infer improvement from selected writing dimensions: under ChatGPT scoring, the experimental group had slightly higher mean sub-scores for clarity (20.3 vs 19.4), logical coherence (18.4 vs 18.0), and use of evidence (17.7 vs 17.0), while instructor ratings favored the control group overall. Because outcomes rely on essay scoring rather than a direct critical-thinking assessment, evidence for durable-skill gains is weak and mixed.
finding.measure: Indirect indicators of critical thinking from essay subscores: clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness
finding.study_size: n=10 total; effective analyzed sample unclear because 2 experimental students were reportedly excluded from final calculations
finding.std_deviation: Subscore SDs reported for ChatGPT assessment only: clarity experimental 2.4 vs control 1.8; use of evidence experimental 1.7 vs control 1.2; logical coherence experimental 1.9 vs control 1.5
